862.title: Block B close: the generation
862.hook: slaves and merchants, poets and nurses, women and men, all of them learners
862.howItsDone: Muslims retell the lives of the companions in sermons, classes and family storytelling, and say 'may God be pleased with him' or 'with her' after a companion's name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Salim, the freed man the Prophet named among four to learn the Qur'an from. Your line was: learn from these four. Who did you thank? Day eight hundred sixty-two.

Lay them out on a table like photographs. A merchant who spent his wealth buying people out of slavery. A man of Abyssinian descent who had been one of those people, calling the prayer. A Persian who traveled from teacher to teacher looking for the truth. A poet. A nurse in a tent. A woman who taught writing. A woman who asked for a day. A shepherd who became a reciter. A man from Yemen who stayed home with his mother. If someone handed you that pile and said, this is one generation, you might ask what holds it together. Today we close the block on the companions.
screen: `A MERCHANT, A CALLER, A SEEKER.` → `A POET, A NURSE, A TEACHER.` → `WHAT HOLDS THEM TOGETHER?`

segments.voice: We started this block with a question: who is a companion? A sahabi, in the common Sunni definition, is someone who met the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, as a believer, and died a believer. That's a wide door, and the people who came through it were not chosen for their background. Walk back through them. The first circle: Abu Bakr and his purchases, Umar walking at night, Uthman and the well of Rumah, Ali and his words. The mothers of the believers: Khadijah, Aisha the scholar, Hafsah keeping the pages, Umm Salamah and the others. The family: Fatimah and her hands, Hasan the peacemaker, Husayn. Then Bilal, Salman, Abu Dharr, Ammar, Mus'ab, Zayd, Usamah, Umm Ayman. The reciters: Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy, Zayd ibn Thabit, Mu'adh. And this last stretch: Abu Hurayrah and Anas, Nusaybah at Uhud, Asma and her two belts, Rufaydah's tent, al-Shifa teaching writing, Umm Sulaym, Hassan the poet, Ka'b who told the truth, Suhayb, Khabbab the blacksmith, Abu Ayyub the host, Sa'd, Abu Musa, Hudhayfah and Salim. And Uways, who by that definition was not a companion at all, since he never met the Prophet, yet whose story sits among theirs. So what holds them together? Look back at story after story and you'll find someone learning. Asking a question. Memorizing a verse. Asking for a day. Asking about harm. Standing behind whoever knew the most Qur'an. Read this way, the companions look like a generation of students. One more honest thing. Muslims don't all remember every one of these names the same way. Sunni and Shia Muslims hold different views about some companions, especially around what happened after the Prophet's death. The next block begins exactly there, and it will set out each telling in its own words.

segments.voice: The practice: write the names you remember. Take a piece of paper, or your notes app. Without looking anything up, write down every companion from this block you can recall. Next to each name, write one thing: a word, a scene, an object. A belt. A tent. A well. A pipe. A mother. Don't worry about the ones you've lost. When the list feels done, read it back slowly. If you pray, you can use the words Muslims say after a companion's name: may God be pleased with them. The bell holds the time.

Sahabi, a companion of the Prophet: someone who met him as a believer and died a believer. This block's close: a generation of very different people, held together by learning and faith. Today's word.
Your line: ordinary people, extraordinary faith. Today, tell one person the story of one companion from your list. Day eight hundred sixty-two.

863.title: The day after
863.hook: as the Prophet ﷺ is prepared for burial, the Ansar and the Muhajirun meet at the portico of Banu Sa'idah
863.howItsDone: Muslims remember the Prophet's death through the reports of that day, and Abu Bakr's words, that God is living and does not die, are quoted at times of loss.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sahabi: the end of the block on the companions. Your line was: ordinary people, extraordinary faith. Whose story did you tell? Today a new block begins, and those same people face the day the Prophet died. Day eight hundred sixty-three.

In a small room beside the mosque in Medina, the body of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, lies still. His family are with him. Outside, the city is in shock. Some people cannot accept it. And a short walk away, under a roofed shelter that belongs to a clan called Banu Sa'idah, men of the Ansar are gathering. They have a question no one in this community has ever had to answer. He is gone. Who leads us now? Today: the day after.
screen: `HIS FAMILY PREPARE HIM.` → `THE CITY IN SHOCK.` → `A GATHERING UNDER A ROOF.`

segments.voice: Sahih al-Bukhari, in a report from Aisha, gives us the hours. When the news spreads, Umar ibn al-Khattab stands up and insists the Prophet has not died. Then Abu Bakr arrives from outside the city. He goes in, uncovers the Prophet's face, kisses him, and says that God will not make him taste death twice. He comes out and speaks to the crowd. Whoever worshipped Muhammad, he says, Muhammad has died. Whoever worships God, God is living and does not die. Then he recites a verse of Surah Al Imran: Muhammad is only a messenger, and messengers passed away before him. If he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels? Ibn Abbas, in a report Bukhari places alongside hers, says it was as if people had never heard the verse until that moment. Meanwhile the Ansar, the people of Medina who had taken the Prophet in, gather at the saqifah of Banu Sa'idah, the roofed portico, around Sa'd ibn Ubadah. Their first proposal, in Bukhari's report, is simple and fair to their eyes: a leader from us, and a leader from you, the Muhajirun who came from Mecca. Word reaches Abu Bakr and Umar, and they go, with Abu Ubaydah. What happens there, and what it means, is where Muslims' memories divide. Sunni Muslims tell it one way, and tomorrow is theirs. Shia Muslims tell it another, and the day after belongs to them. Today, stay with the hour before any answer. A community has lost the one who received revelation. The family is with his body. Grief and fear and duty are all in the air at once. And everyone is asking the same two words.
screen: `UMAR: HE HAS NOT DIED.` · `ABU BAKR: GOD IS LIVING.` · `THE ANSAR GATHER AT THE SAQIFAH.` · `A LEADER FROM US, AND FROM YOU.` · then, large: `WHAT NOW?`

segments.voice: The practice: sit with the sudden loss of a leader. Sit still for a moment, and let your breath find its pace. Remember a time someone who held things together was suddenly gone. A parent. A coach. A boss. An imam or teacher. Notice what that hour was like. The shock. The practical questions arriving before the grief had room. People reacting in different ways at once. Breathe in, and let both be true: the loss, and the need to go on. Breathe out, without rushing to an answer. If you pray, you can pray for those who lead your community, and for those who grieve. The bell holds the time.
Saqifah. The roofed shelter where the Ansar met, the day the Prophet died, to ask who would lead, while his family stayed with his body. Today's word.

864.title: The Sunni telling
864.hook: Sunni Muslims hold that the community chose Abu Bakr by consultation and pledge
864.howItsDone: Sunni Muslims honor Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali as the rightly guided caliphs, and Sunni scholars discuss consultation (shura) and the pledge (bay'ah) when they write about leadership.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the day after: the Prophet's family preparing him for burial, and the Ansar gathering at the saqifah. Your line was: what now? Today, one community's answer, in its own words. Day eight hundred sixty-four.

Under the roof of the saqifah the voices are rising. A leader from us and a leader from you, the Ansar have said. Abu Bakr has spoken, and he has put forward two other men, Umar and Abu Ubaydah, and said: pledge to whichever of them you choose. Then Umar, by his own account in Sahih al-Bukhari, turns to Abu Bakr and says: stretch out your hand. Abu Bakr does. Umar places his hand in it and pledges. Others follow. This is how Sunni Muslims tell what happened next. Today's word: khalifah.
screen: `A LEADER FROM US, AND FROM YOU.` → `ABU BAKR PUTS FORWARD TWO.` → `STRETCH OUT YOUR HAND.`

segments.voice: Khalifah is usually rendered successor or deputy, one who comes after and stands in for another. The Qur'an uses the word in its second surah, when God tells the angels, in Pickthall's translation: "Lo! I am about to place a viceroy in the earth." Abu Bakr came to be called the khalifah of the Messenger of God, his successor in leading the community, though not in prophecy. Revelation had ended with the Prophet. So how was he chosen? Sunni Muslims hold that the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, did not formally name a successor, and that the community chose. They point to the pledge, the bay'ah, given hand in hand at the saqifah. They point to a second, wider pledge, which Bukhari reports was taken from the people in the mosque the following day. And they point to signs of Abu Bakr's standing: when the Prophet was too ill to lead the prayer, Bukhari reports he told the people to let Abu Bakr lead it. Sunni scholars also look to a Qur'anic description of the believers as those "whose affairs are a matter of counsel." Consultation, shura, and pledge became, in this telling, the way the community chose. The telling is honest about the strain, too. Umar himself, later, as leader of the believers, says in Bukhari that the pledge to Abu Bakr was made in haste, and that God protected the community from its harm. He warns that no one should take a pledge without the counsel of the believers. For Sunni Muslims, then, Abu Bakr is the first of the caliphs, chosen by people who knew him. Tomorrow, the Shia telling, in its own words.

segments.voice: The practice: learn how your community chooses leaders. Breathe out slowly, then once more. Bring to mind a community you belong to. A mosque, a church, a school board, a club, a family business, a group of friends. Ask yourself: how does someone come to lead here? Who gets asked? Who gets heard? Is there a pledge, a vote, a quiet understanding? Breathe in, and notice what you actually know. Breathe out, and notice what you don't. If you pray, you can pray for wisdom for whoever leads it. The bell holds the time.

865.title: The Shia telling
865.hook: Shia Muslims hold that the Prophet ﷺ had designated Ali, by God's command, as his successor
865.howItsDone: Shia Muslims hold Ali ibn Abi Talib to be the first imam after the Prophet, designated by God, and remember the imams of the Prophet's family in prayers, visits and commemorations.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sunni telling, and the word khalifah. Your line was: chosen by pledge. What did you learn about how a leader near you was chosen? Today, the other telling, in its own words. Day eight hundred sixty-five.

Go back into the small room beside the mosque. Ali ibn Abi Talib, the Prophet's cousin and the husband of his daughter Fatimah, is with the family, washing the body of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and preparing him for burial. He is not at the saqifah. In the Shia telling, it is while he is here that a leader is pledged to without him. For Shia Muslims, that scene carries the weight of the whole story. The question was not open, they hold. It had already been answered. Today's word: imam.
screen: `ALI IS WITH THE BODY.` → `NOT AT THE SAQIFAH.` → `ALREADY ANSWERED, THEY HOLD.`

segments.voice: Imam, in everyday Muslim life, is the one who stands in front and leads the prayer. In Shia teaching it also names something larger: the rightful leader of the community after the Prophet, appointed by God, not elected by people. Shia Muslims hold that the Prophet designated Ali by God's command, and that Ali was the first imam. The word for that designation is nass, an explicit appointment. Where do they look? They point to the Qur'an's account of Abraham. God tells him: I will make you an imam for the people. Abraham asks, and from my descendants? And God answers that His covenant does not reach the wrongdoers. Shia scholars read in this that leadership of this kind is God's to give. They point to a report that Sunni collections also carry, in Bukhari and Muslim. When the Prophet left Ali behind in Medina during an expedition, Ali was troubled, and the Prophet asked him: are you not content to be to me as Harun was to Musa, except that there is no prophet after me? Sunni scholars read that as a sign of love and trust on that occasion. Shia scholars read in it a standing rank, a deputy and successor. Same words. Two readings. And they point to the hours we saw two days ago. Bukhari itself reports that Ali did not give his pledge to Abu Bakr for a time. For Shia Muslims, that holding back says something. What both sides share matters too. Sunni and Shia Muslims both love and honor Ali. The disagreement is about what was given to him, and when. Tomorrow, words that both traditions report, spoken at a place called Ghadir Khumm.

If neither is yours, pick any view you've never really listened to, in your family or your town. Breathe in, and say it to yourself as its holders would say it, at its strongest. Breathe out, and notice what moves in you. You don't have to agree. Just listen all the way to the end. The bell holds the time.

866.title: Ghadir Khumm
866.hook: both traditions report the Prophet ﷺ saying, of whomever I am his mawla, Ali is his mawla, and they read it differently
866.howItsDone: Sunni and Shia Muslims both narrate the hadith of Ghadir Khumm; Shia Muslims celebrate Eid al-Ghadir as the day the Prophet designated Ali, while Sunni scholars teach it as a call to love and support Ali.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Shia telling, and the word imam. Your line was: designated, they say. Did you let someone finish their whole point? Day eight hundred sixty-six.

A watering place on the road between Mecca and Medina, called Khumm. Tradition knows the spot as Ghadir Khumm, the pool of Khumm. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, stops there with the people traveling with him. He stands up to speak. Sahih Muslim records the scene through the companion Zayd ibn Arqam. The Prophet says he is only a human being, and that the messenger of his Lord will soon come for him. He is speaking like someone saying goodbye. Today: Ghadir Khumm.
screen: `A POOL ON THE ROAD.` → `HE STANDS TO SPEAK.` → `LIKE SOMEONE SAYING GOODBYE.`

segments.voice: In Muslim's report, the Prophet goes on: I am leaving among you two weighty things. The first is the Book of God, in which is guidance and light, so hold fast to it. The second is the people of my house. And he says, more than once: I remind you of God concerning the people of my house. Then there is the line at the center of today. Al-Tirmidhi records it: of whomever I am his mawla, Ali is his mawla. Sunni and Shia collections both carry these words. Sunni and Shia Muslims both honor them. And they read them differently, because of one word. Mawla carries more than one meaning. A few days ago it described Salim, the freed man linked to Abu Hudhayfah's house. Readers of this hadith have heard in it friend, ally, protector, patron, or master. In the Sunni reading, it means love and loyalty here: whoever loves me and takes me as his friend should love and stand by Ali. Some of them connect it to a tension reported in Bukhari: Buraydah, who had been with Ali on a mission, resented him, and the Prophet told him not to hate Ali. In this reading, Ghadir is a public defense of Ali and a call to love him. Shia Muslims read mawla here as master, the one with authority over the believers. In their reading, the Prophet is naming his successor in front of the people, by God's command, and the words about his household point the same way. Shia communities mark the day as a festival, Eid al-Ghadir. Same pool. Same sentence. Two readings, held with deep conviction, and each with its scholars and its reasons.

Breathe out. Don't choose. Notice how a single word can carry a whole history, and how much careful listening a sentence can ask of us. If you pray, you can ask for understanding. 867.title: Fatimah's last months
867.hook: the Prophet's daughter dies within months of her father, and her grief is remembered by Sunni and Shia Muslims alike
867.howItsDone: Sunni and Shia Muslims both honor Fatimah as the Prophet's daughter; Sunnis usually follow her name with 'may God be pleased with her' and Shia Muslims with 'peace be upon her', and her life and grief are retold in sermons and gatherings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ghadir Khumm: one sentence about Ali, and two communities reading it two ways. Your line was: the same words, two readings. When a sentence divided two people you know, did you ask each what the key word meant to them? Day eight hundred sixty-seven.

A sick room in Medina. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is in his last illness, and his daughter Fatimah comes in. Aisha, who is there, later says that Fatimah walked exactly the way her father walked. He welcomes her and sits her beside him. Then he leans in and whispers something, and Fatimah cries. He leans in again and whispers a second time, and she laughs. Aisha asks her what he said. Fatimah won't tell. Not yet. She keeps the secret until after he has died. Today, the months that came after that whisper.
screen: `A WHISPER, AND SHE CRIES.` → `A SECOND WHISPER, AND SHE LAUGHS.` → `SHE KEEPS THE SECRET.`

segments.voice: When Aisha asks again, after the Prophet's death, Fatimah tells her. The first whisper: he had told her that he would die of this illness. So she cried. The second whisper: he had told her that she would be the first of his household to follow him. So she laughed. Sit with that for a second. The news that she would die soon is the news that made her laugh. Bukhari and Muslim both record it, and in the same report he tells her she will be a leader among the women of Paradise. Then come the days of grief. Bukhari records that as his illness grew heavy, Fatimah said, oh, the pain my father is in. And he answered her gently: there will be no more pain for your father after today. When he died, she spoke to him the way a daughter does, calling him again and again, oh my father. And after the burial she turned to Anas and asked how they could bring themselves to pour earth over the Messenger of God. There is no theory in that question. It is a daughter at a grave. In those same months, Bukhari also records, Fatimah asked Abu Bakr for her share of what her father had left, and he answered with a saying of the Prophet that prophets leave no inheritance. Sunni and Shia Muslims read that exchange very differently, and both traditions remember her grief. The same report says she lived on for months after her father, not years. She followed him soon, as the second whisper had said. Shia Muslims honor her among the Ma'sumin, the ones they hold were kept free of sin, and Sunni Muslims honor her as the Prophet's beloved daughter and a leader of the women of Paradise. Different words. The same tears at the same grave.

segments.voice: The practice: remember Fatimah. Let your shoulders drop, and picture the room: a father who knows he is dying, a daughter beside him, two whispers. Breathe in, and think how short the time was. Breathe out. If you pray, you can ask peace and mercy for her in your own words. Sunni Muslims often say, may God be pleased with her; Shia Muslims often say, peace be upon her. If you don't pray, simply hold her name for a moment, and the name of someone you've lost. The bell holds the time.

Your line: she followed him soon. Today, tell someone you love one thing you'd want them to know, and don't wait for the last whisper. Day eight hundred sixty-seven.

868.title: Abu Bakr's first speech
868.hook: obey me as long as I obey Allah, and if I go wrong, set me right (sirah)
868.howItsDone: Abu Bakr's first address is often quoted by Sunni Muslims in sermons and teaching about leadership, especially its lines asking the people to help him when he does well and set him right when he does wrong.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Fatimah: two whispers, a grave, and a daughter who followed her father soon. Your line was: she followed him soon. Did you say the thing you didn't want to leave unsaid? Day eight hundred sixty-eight.

A new leader stands up in front of the people for the first time. What does a person usually say in that moment? Something about strength. Something about a plan. Something about how things are going to be better now. Abu Bakr, the Prophet's longtime friend, has just received the pledge of the community in Medina. Sunni Muslims remember this as the moment he took office as caliph; Shia Muslims, as this week has shown, remember the succession differently. Either way, the speech the sources give him is short, and it doesn't sound like a victory speech at all. It sounds like a man asking to be watched. Today: Abu Bakr's first speech.
screen: `A NEW LEADER STANDS UP.` → `NO VICTORY SPEECH.` → `A MAN ASKING TO BE WATCHED.`

segments.voice: The speech comes to us through the sirah, the early biographies of the Prophet, in the work of Ibn Ishaq as passed on by Ibn Hisham. In paraphrase, it goes like this. I have been put in charge of you, and I am not the best of you. If I do well, help me. If I do wrong, set me right. Truthfulness is a trust, and lying is a betrayal. The weak among you is strong in my eyes until I get him his right, and the strong among you is weak in my eyes until I take from him what he owes. Obey me as long as I obey God and His Messenger, and if I disobey them, you owe me no obedience. Take it a line at a time. First, I am not the best of you. He opens by lowering himself, not raising himself. Second, set me right. He is handing the people the job of correcting him. Third, the weak and the strong. Power usually leans toward the strong. He says it will lean the other way until rights are paid. And fourth, the limit. Obedience has an edge: it stops where he stops obeying God. A leader who writes his own limit into his first words is telling the people where the line is before anyone has to find it. In Sunni teaching, this speech is read as a picture of how authority should sit on a person: lightly, and under God.
screen: `I AM NOT THE BEST OF YOU.` · `IF I DO WRONG, SET ME RIGHT.` · `THE WEAK ARE STRONG WITH ME.` · `NO OBEDIENCE IF I DISOBEY GOD.` · then, large: `SET ME RIGHT.`

segments.voice: The practice: invite correction. Sit back, and let a breath out slowly. Think of one place where you have a little authority. At work, at home, over a younger sibling, in a group chat you run. Breathe in, and ask yourself honestly: who would tell me if I were getting this wrong? Breathe out. Pick one person you trust, and decide, here in the quiet, that you'll ask them this week: is there anything I should be doing differently? Hold the question until it stops feeling dangerous. The bell holds the time.
Abu Bakr. The Prophet's longtime friend, who in his first speech as leader said: I am not the best of you; if I do well, help me; if I do wrong, set me right. Today's word.

Your line: set me right. Today, ask one person to tell you where you could do better, and thank them for the answer. And look back at the week: the generation, saqifah, two tellings, Ghadir Khumm, Fatimah, and a leader asking to be corrected. Day eight hundred sixty-eight.
